hmmt-feb-1999-adv-01.title: Divisibility by 8 and 9
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-01.body:
The total in cents is the 5-digit number $\overline{a999b}$, and it is a multiple of $72=8\cdot 9$.

- Divisible by 8: the last three digits $99b$ must be divisible by 8, so $b=2$ ($992=8\cdot 124$).
- Divisible by 9: the digit sum $a+9+9+9+2=a+29$ must be a multiple of 9, so $a=7$.

The total is $\$799.92$, and $799.92/72=11.11$.

**Answer: \$11.11**

hmmt-feb-1999-adv-02.title: Work backwards
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-02.body:
Before the last shop she had $1024$, so before the lottery just ahead of it she had $512$. Before the previous shop she had $512+1024=1536$, so before its lottery $768$, and so on.

Let $m_k$ be the amount she holds just before the lottery that precedes the $k$-th shop counted from the end. Then $m_1=512$ and $m_{k+1}=\frac{m_k+1024}{2}$, i.e. $1024-m_{k+1}=\frac{1024-m_k}{2}$.

So $1024-m_k=2^{10-k}$, and $d=m_{10}=1024-2^{0}=1023$.

**Answer: 1023**

hmmt-feb-1999-adv-02.title: Run it forwards
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-02.body:
With $d$ dollars, after the $n$-th shop she has $2^n d-1024(2^{n-1}+\dots+2+1)=2^nd-1024(2^n-1)$. Setting this to $0$ for $n=10$ gives $d=1024\cdot\frac{2^{10}-1}{2^{10}}=1023$.

**Answer: 1023**

hmmt-feb-1999-adv-03.title: Set up an equation
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-03.body:
Let $p$ be the probability of heads. There are $\binom42=6$ orders with 2 heads and 2 tails, each of probability $p^2(1-p)^2$, and $\binom43=4$ orders with 3 heads and 1 tail, each of probability $p^3(1-p)$.

So $6p^2(1-p)^2=4p^3(1-p)$. The common probability is nonzero, so $p\ne0,1$ and we may divide by $p^2(1-p)$: $6(1-p)=4p$, giving $p=\frac35$.

**Answer: $\frac35$**

hmmt-feb-1999-adv-04.title: Count inversions
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-04.body:
Every pair of pieces starts in the wrong relative order, and there are $\binom{16}{2}=120$ pairs. One adjacent switch changes the relative order of exactly one pair, so at least $120$ switches are needed.

Bubble sort achieves it: move $1$ to the front with 15 switches, then $2$ to the second place with 14 switches, and so on, for $15+14+\dots+1=120$ switches in total.

**Answer: 120**

hmmt-feb-1999-adv-05.title: Count how often each element appears
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-05.body:
Each element of $S$ lies in exactly $2^{1998}$ subsets $E$ (the other 1998 elements are free). Hence $\sum_E f(E)=2^{1998}\,f(S)$, and the requested sum is $\dfrac{2^{1998}f(S)}{f(S)}=2^{1998}$.

**Answer: $2^{1998}$**

hmmt-feb-1999-adv-05.title: Pair subsets with complements
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-05.body:
Subsets $E$ and $S\setminus E$ satisfy $f(E)+f(S\setminus E)=f(S)$, so each pair contributes $1$ to the sum. There are $2^{1999}/2=2^{1998}$ pairs, so the sum is $2^{1998}$.

**Answer: $2^{1998}$**

hmmt-feb-1999-adv-06.title: Use the least common multiple
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-06.body:
The number $N$ of sheets satisfies $N\equiv1$ modulo each of $2,\dots,8$, so $N-1$ is a multiple of $\operatorname{lcm}(2,\dots,8)=840$. With $1000<N<2000$ the only option is $N=1681=41^2$.

Piles of equal size, neither one pile nor piles of a single sheet, means a number of piles that is a divisor of $1681$ other than $1$ and $1681$. The only one is $41$.

**Answer: 41**

hmmt-feb-1999-adv-07.title: Factor $x^3-343$
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-07.body:
A number whose cube is $343$ is a root of $x^3-343=(x-7)(x^2+7x+49)$. The non-real ones are the roots of $x^2+7x+49$ (discriminant $49-196<0$), which is of the required form $x^2+ax+b$ with real $a,b$.

**Answer: $(a,b)=(7,49)$**

hmmt-feb-1999-adv-07.title: Use $7\omega$
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-07.body:
The non-real cube roots of $343$ are $7\omega$ and $7\bar\omega$ with $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$. Their sum is $7(\omega+\bar\omega)=-7$ and their product is $49$, so the quadratic is $x^2+7x+49$.

**Answer: $(7,49)$**

hmmt-feb-1999-adv-08.title: Place $S$ in the narrow wedge
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-08.body:
The center of $S$ lies on a bisector of one of the angles formed by the diameters, at distance $d$ from the center $O$ of $C$ where $\sin(\theta/2)=1/d$ and $\theta$ is the angle of the wedge containing $S$. Internal tangency gives $R=d+1$. To make $R$ largest, make $d$ largest, i.e. use the narrow wedge $\theta=30^\circ$: $d=\frac1{\sin15^\circ}$.

Since $\sin15^\circ=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}$, $d=\frac{4}{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}=\sqrt6+\sqrt2$.

So $R=1+\sqrt2+\sqrt6$.

**Answer: $1+\sqrt2+\sqrt6$**

hmmt-feb-1999-adv-09.title: Bayes' theorem
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-09.body:
Counterfeit coins are $1\%$ of all coins and the scale catches $95\%$ of them, so $0.95\%$ of all coins are counterfeit and sent to the lab. Since $5\%$ of all coins are sent, a coin at the lab is counterfeit with probability $\frac{0.95}{5}=19\%$ and real with probability $81\%$.

The lab says \"counterfeit\" for a counterfeit coin with probability $0.9$ and for a real coin with probability $0.1$. Hence
$$P=\frac{0.19\cdot0.9}{0.19\cdot0.9+0.81\cdot0.1}=\frac{0.171}{0.252}=\frac{19}{28}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{19}{28}$**

hmmt-feb-1999-adv-10.title: Sum is 1 and a discriminant bound
hmmt-feb-1999-adv-10.body:
Let $s=x+y$, $p=xy$. The three quantities are $p$, $1-s+p$ and $s-2p$, and they add up to $1$. Real $x,y$ require $s^2\ge4p$.

Suppose all three were less than $\frac49$. Since they sum to $1$, each would then exceed $1-2\cdot\frac49=\frac19$; in particular $\frac19<p<\frac49$.

But $s-2p<\frac49$ gives $s<\frac49+2p$, so $0\le s^2-4p<(\frac49+2p)^2-4p$, i.e. $0<p^2-\frac59p+\frac4{81}=(p-\frac19)(p-\frac49)$, which forces $p<\frac19$ or $p>\frac49$. Contradiction. So the largest of the three is always at least $\frac49$.

Equality: $x=y=\frac13$ gives $xy=\frac19$, $1-x-y+xy=\frac49$, $x+y-2xy=\frac49$.

**Answer: $\frac49$**
